title: Julia Quick Reference
description: Look up a lesson idea, see its small example, and check a common mistake. Open the linked lesson for setup and practice steps.

entries.name: Print a greeting
entries.summary: println prints a value followed by a newline.

entries.name: Keep a named number
entries.summary: A variable gives a name to a value. The plus sign adds numbers.
notes: Quoted numbers are text, not values for ordinary arithmetic.

entries.name: Build a message
entries.summary: A dollar sign inserts a variable into a string.

entries.name: Read an array item
entries.summary: Julia arrays normally start at position 1.
notes: A position outside the array raises an error.

entries.name: Apply an action to every item
entries.summary: A dot applies an operation element by element. Here each number is doubled.
notes: The dot is important when you want item-by-item operations.

entries.name: Choose an action
entries.summary: if selects steps using a true-or-false rule. end closes the block.

example.code:
score = 8
if score >= 5
 println("Pass")
else
 println("Try again")
end

notes: Julia requires a Boolean condition, not a bare number.

entries.name: Visit a range
entries.summary: 1:3 is a range including both ends. A for loop visits each value.

entries.name: Name a short calculation
entries.summary: A short function definition can use an equals sign. The expression is returned.
notes: Calling a function needs parentheses around its inputs.

entries.name: Use a named key
entries.summary: Dict connects keys with values. The => pair operator joins a key and value.
notes: Missing bracket keys throw an error; get can supply a fallback.

entries.name: Group fixed values
entries.summary: A tuple is a fixed group of values. You can unpack its positions into names.
notes: A tuple itself cannot be changed item by item.

entries.name: Build a list with a rule
entries.summary: A comprehension makes values from inputs and an optional filter.

example.code: println([n * 2 for n in 1:4 if n > 2])

notes: Read the filter before working out which values are included.

entries.name: Group named fields
entries.summary: A struct defines a type with named fields. Ordinary structs are immutable.

example.code:
struct Book
 title::String
 pages::Int
end
book = Book("Moon Trip", 24)
println(book.pages)

notes: Use mutable struct only when fields really need changing.
